title: Fence Stain Calculator: How Much Stain for a Fence
description: Work out fence stain in gallons from length, height, sides, and coats. Label coverage is 200 to 400 sq ft per gallon. See a full example.

keywords: how much stain for a fence
takeaways: Fence area is length x height x number of sides, and most fences need stain on both sides.
Behr and Sherwin-Williams labels put solid stain coverage at 200 to 400 sq ft per gallon, with rough old wood near 200.
Plan on two coats for solid color stain, and round gallons up so you do not run short mid-fence.
body:
For a 100 ft long, 6 ft tall fence stained on both sides with two coats, plan on about 12 gallons at the rough wood rate of 200 sq ft per gallon. Your fence size, how many sides you stain, wood condition, and coats decide the real count, so run the area math first and pick a coverage rate from the can label.

## The formula for fence stain

**Gallons = length (ft) x height (ft) x sides x coats / coverage per gallon, rounded up.**

Coverage is the part people guess wrong. Behr lists its exterior wood stain at 200 to 400 sq ft per gallon. Sherwin-Williams lists SuperDeck solid color stain at 200 to 400 sq ft per gallon at 4 to 8 mils wet, with two coats and no more than two coats. Smooth new wood drinks less and lands near the high end. Rough sawn, dry, or old wood drinks more and lands near 200 sq ft per gallon, and semi-transparent stain can cover less on rough wood.

| Wood and job | Planning coverage per gallon |
| --- | --- |
| Smooth new wood, one even coat | 350 to 400 sq ft |
| Average fence boards, sound wood | 250 to 300 sq ft |
| Rough sawn or dry old wood | 200 to 250 sq ft |
| First coat on very dry wood | Use 200 sq ft to be safe |

The fence stain calculator above takes fence size, wood condition, and coats, then shows gallons and cost. Wood condition sets the coverage rate in the tool, which is why you pick honest condition, not best case. If you spray, plan a bit more. Spraying is fast, but wind loss and back-brushing still use stain, and the label tells you to back-brush sprayed stain for an even coat.

Pick your stain type before you buy. Transparent stain shows all the grain and fades fastest. Semi-transparent adds color and still shows grain. Solid color hides grain and flaws and lasts longest on a fence, but it can peel if the wood was wet or dirty at coat time. Most fence jobs use semi-transparent or solid.

## Worked example: a 100 ft fence, 6 ft tall, both sides, two coats

Your fence is a cedar privacy fence, 100 ft long and 6 ft tall (30.5 x 1.8 m). The wood is rough and dry, last stained years ago. You will stain both sides with a solid color stain, two coats, as the Sherwin-Williams SuperDeck label directs.

Step 1, area for one side. 100 ft x 6 ft = 600 sq ft.

Step 2, both sides. 600 x 2 sides = 1,200 sq ft of wood.

Step 3, two coats. 1,200 x 2 coats = 2,400 sq ft of coat area to cover.

Step 4, gallons at the rough wood rate. Use 200 sq ft per gallon from the low end of the Behr and Sherwin-Williams label range. 2,400 / 200 = 12.0 gallons. Rounded up like a buyer, you need 12 gallons.

Step 5, check the math a second way. One side, one coat at 200 sq ft per gallon is 600 / 200 = 3 gallons. There are 2 sides and 2 coats, so 3 x 2 x 2 = 12 gallons, which matches Step 4.

Step 6, check the one-side case. If your neighbor side is not yours to stain, cut the job in half: 600 sq ft x 2 coats / 200 = 6 gallons. Gates count too. A 4 ft wide gate at 6 ft tall adds 24 sq ft per side, small on this job, but count it on a short fence.

Buy the 12 gallons as two 5 gallon pails plus two single gallons if your store stocks that mix, and keep one gallon sealed as a touch-up can if the price break on pails is good. Mix pails of the same color in a big bucket first, a step called boxing, so color stays even from pail to pail. Our [fence calculator](/blog/fence-calculator/) helps with post and picket counts if you are building the fence as well as staining it.

## How to measure a fence for stain

Walk the fence with a tape and add up each run in feet. Break an L-shaped yard into straight runs. Measure height at the boards, not at the post tops. Most privacy fences are 6 ft.

Decide on sides up front and talk to your neighbor. If the fence is shared, agree on color and cost split before you buy. A HOA can also set color rules, so check first.

Count picket gaps honestly. A spaced picket fence has less wood than length x height. As a rough guide, a picket fence with 2 in gaps on 5.5 in pickets has about 73 percent board coverage, so use area x 0.73 before coats.

Posts and rails add a small amount. On a board fence they sit inside the length x height face, so most owners skip a post count and rely on rounding up.

## Mistakes that make you run short or peel early

The top mistake is counting one side and one coat, then buying half the stain you need. The worked example shows how fast the count grows: 3 gallons for one side and one coat turns into 12 gallons for two sides and two coats at the same rate.

Staining dirty or wet wood is next. Wash the fence, let it dry 24 to 48 hours, and test with a splash of water. If water beads, wait. If it soaks in, you are ready. Behr prep steps call for a wood cleaner on weathered wood and stripping a failed old coat first.

Over-applying is a real fault. Heavy coats can peel and crack, and the SuperDeck label says never apply more than two coats of its solid stain. Use thin, even coats, keep a wet edge, and back-brush. The Behr label says apply between 40 and 90 degrees F and skip the job if rain is due within 24 hours.

Test one board at the back with your full coat count before you open all the pails. For house paint amounts, see our [exterior paint calculator](/blog/exterior-paint-calculator/).

## Frequently asked questions

### How much stain do I need for a 100 ft fence?
A 100 ft by 6 ft fence is 600 sq ft per side. Both sides with two coats at 200 sq ft per gallon needs 12 gallons. One side with two coats needs 6 gallons.

### How much does one gallon of fence stain cover?
Labels for Behr exterior stain and Sherwin-Williams SuperDeck solid stain both list 200 to 400 sq ft per gallon. Plan near 200 for rough or dry wood and near 350 to 400 for smooth new wood.

### Do I need one coat or two coats of fence stain?
Solid color stain labels call for two coats for full coverage and color. Many semi-transparent stains go on in one coat, with a second coat for deeper color if the label allows it. Read your can, because some products forbid a third coat.

### How long does fence stain last before a recoat?
A fence in full sun often needs a recoat in 2 to 4 years for transparent and semi-transparent stains, and longer for solid color. Shade, sprinklers that wet the fence daily, and soil piled on the bottom boards all shorten that time.

### Can I spray fence stain instead of brushing?
Yes, with an airless sprayer, but back-brush or back-roll at once for an even coat, as the Behr label directs. Mask plants, walls, and concrete first, and plan a bit more stain for wind loss.

### Should I stain a new fence right away?
Wait until the wood is dry and takes water evenly. New pressure treated boards can need several weeks of dry weather. Do the splash test: if water soaks in across the board, the wood is ready.
